rv.q: I rarely leave the theatre feeling so deeply impacted and, frankly, galvanised by what I've seen.
Williams and Pearson's unflinching direction is most compelling in its bleak brutality.
But this is still a searing experience that asks provocative, if familiar questions about the price we pay to perform the parts demanded of us – on stage, or off.
NINA is one of those rare productions that gets under your skin.
In a post #MeToo era, NINA is a meta theatrical fever dream on coercion, power and the quest for creative expression.
NINA offers a rich exploration of The Seagull by rewarding those familiar with the original.
NINA is a timely return to issues never properly addressed.
Bold, playful and deliberately unpredictable, it embraces the possibilities of experimental theatre while confronting the uneasy relationship between performance, power and control.
The finish mars what otherwise is a compelling and challenging piece of work that’s also very well acted.
A fierce exploration of acting and misogyny featuring fabulous performances, theatrical chaos and dark comedy that’s perhaps overly constrained by conventional storytelling.
NINA most brilliantly represents the insidious, frog-in-boiling-water nature of manipulation and exploitation in the real world.

cn.t: Critics praise this fierce, gripping exploration of power dynamics and exploitation in theater, with reviewers calling it a rare production that stays with you and successfully repurposes Chekhov's "The Seagull" into something genuinely relevant for today.
